name: Identity & consistency

pinned_evidence.title: Compliance without pressure: The foot-in-the-door technique

evidence.basis: People are motivated to act consistently with their self-image and prior commitments (self-perception theory, Bem; foot-in-the-door, Freedman & Fraser 1966). Identity-based motivation (Oyserman) shows people act in line with salient identities.
evidence.effect_size_note: Consistency and identity effects are real; foot-in-the-door is a classic but with moderate and somewhat variable replication. Identity-based motivation is well-supported when the identity is genuinely salient and self-relevant.

mechanism_summary_for_context: People strive to act consistently with who they believe they are and what they've already committed to. Two levers: invite a small genuine commitment or self-definition early (a stated goal, a chosen identity, a small first action) and later actions align with it; and make a relevant identity salient ('you're a builder') so behavior follows the identity. The identity and commitments must be genuine and user-chosen, not imposed or manipulated.

preconditions.reason: requires a real self-chosen goal, identity, or commitment; not applicable where none is genuinely elicited

applicability.culture_note: Consistency motivation is broadly present but its strength (individualist consistency pressure vs collectivist context-sensitivity) varies; an L3 surface parameter

implementations.generation_directive: Have the user state a genuine goal or self-definition early ('What do you want to build?', 'I'm here to {goal}'). The stated commitment, freely chosen, anchors later behavior toward consistency. Reflect it back later ('You said you wanted to {goal} — here's your next step'). Never put words in the user's mouth or manufacture commitments they didn't make.

Make a genuine, self-relevant identity salient in a way that supports the user's own goals ('You're a founder', 'You're a creator') where it truly reflects them. Identity framing motivates aligned action. Do not impose identities the user hasn't embraced or use identity to manipulate against their interest.

hard_rules.rule: Commitments and stated goals must be genuinely made by the user; fabricating or implying commitments the user did not make is forbidden
Do not impose or manipulate identities the user hasn't embraced, or weaponize self-image against the user's interest
Do not use prior small commitments to escalate into significantly larger unwanted ones (manipulative foot-in-the-door); escalation must be reasonable and user-serving

constraints.boundary_test: Is this reinforcing a goal or identity the user genuinely chose — or manufacturing commitment and manipulating self-image?

relations.note: 'Mine' (endowment) shades into 'part of who I am' (identity); distinct drivers — ownership valuation vs self-consistency
A stated goal creates a progress target; distinct — ID-12 is self-consistency, ZE-07 is goal-gradient progress

reference_examples.what: User states a learning goal and daily commitment up front; later nudges reference that self-chosen commitment
Identity-based framing motivates behavior consistent with the embraced identity

reference_examples.product: Ventora onboarding ('What do you want to build?')
reference_examples.what: Eliciting a genuine goal early anchors the build journey to the user's stated intent
